title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
summary:
The M5-powered MacBook Air is $300 off in both size configurations for Black Friday. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge	

If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.
Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)

Where to Buy:

 $1299 $999 at Amazon (512GB)
 $1299 $999 at Best Buy (512GB)
 $1599 $1199 at Amazon (1TB)


Apple MacBook Air 15 (M5)

Where to Buy:

 $1299 $1199 at Amazon (512GB)
 $1299 $1199 at Best Buy (512GB)
 $1799 $1499 at Amazon (1TB)

The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount, is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.
Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.
Read our M5-powered MacBook Air review.

title: Event Horizon Telescope views the dynamics and geometry of a black hole jet in extreme detail
summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. summary: The last few days we've been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently—maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution?

summary: The mucus layer in the human gut is a tough place for bacteria: nutrients are scarce, and conditions are harsh. How do bacteria adapt to such extreme environments? AirPods Pro 3

 $449 $349 at Amazon (GPS, 46mm)

Read our review.

Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

 $29 $18 at Amazon
 $29 $18 at Walmart
 $29 $18 at Best Buy

It was one of the fastest wireless chargers we tested, bringing an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65 percent in an hour. Read our guide to the best Qi2 batteries.

 $79.99 $51.99 at Amazon (orange)
 $79.99 $56.98 at Amazon (black)
 $79.99 $59.99 at Amazon (pink)


Apple iPad (11th-gen)
Apple’s 11th-gen iPad offers 128GB of storage — twice that of its predecessor — and runs on a faster A16 chip. It also comes in four colors: blue, pink, yellow, and silver.

Where to Buy:

 $449 $379 at Amazon (128GB, Wi-Fi)
 $449 $379 at Walmart (128GB, Wi-Fi)

You can buy the last-gen iPad Mini with 128GB of storage and Wi-Fi on Amazon in select colors for $484 ($115 off), which is the best price we’ve seen since Apple’s recent price hikes. It has a smaller screen and a slower chip than the newer model, and it lacks an OLED screen, the Acoustic Display, and water resistance. Still, it’s a great option for reading and everyday use that’s currently more affordable than its $599 successor, with support for Apple Intelligence and the Apple Pencil Pro. Read our review.
Apple’s latest Magic Mouse is matching its all-time low of $59.99 ($20 off) at Amazon. The wireless mouse features a touch-sensitive surface that lets you scroll through documents and swipe between apps with simple gestures; it also pairs automatically with compatible Macs and offers support for USB-C.
Apple Pencil (USB-C)
Apple’s entry-level stylus attaches magnetically to supported iPads, though it doesn’t support magnetic charging. Instead, you pair and charge it by connecting it to your device’s USB-C port. It includes tilt sensitivity and Apple Pencil Hover support, but it doesn’t offer double-tap gestures or pressure sensitivity.

Where to Buy:

 $79 $49 at Amazon
 $79 $49 at Walmart
 $79 $49 at Best Buy


Sharge Icemag 3 Power Bank
The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.

Where to Buy:

 $79.9 $63.9 at Amazon (black)
 $79.9 $63.9 at Amazon (white)
 $79.9 $63.9 at Sharge


Apple Studio Display (2026)
Designed to pair with a Mac, the latest Apple Studio Display features a sharp 5K Retina display, a great 12-megapixel Center Stage camera that keeps you in frame during video calls, and a good six-speaker sound system with spatial audio. Sadly, it only offers two Thunderbolt 5 ports in addition to a pair of USB-C ports. Read our review.


Where to Buy:

 $1599 $1399 at Amazon

title: BepiColombo safely in Mercury orbit despite unexpected challenge
summary:
On 21 November, starting at 18:24 UTC, BepiColombo achieved Mercury orbit insertion (MOI), the second major milestone of its planetary arrival phase. As soon as the signal from the spacecraft was re-established after a scheduled loss of contact, the Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, saw that the spacecraft had entered safe mode. 

 An issue occurred during the thruster burn, causing the manoeuvre to end earlier than expected. Since then, teams at ESOC have been working around the clock with lead spacecraft manufacturer Airbus and colleagues across the joint ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission to investigate the issue, which has been traced to a software glitch. 

BepiColombo is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury – an important milestone after its eight-year journey to the planet – and is on track for the separation of its two science orbiters on 9 December in Germany (10 December in Japan). 

The mission also delivered a first: entering orbit around another planet using ‘weak stability capture’. This involves arriving at lower speeds than is typical for planetary missions, and is a technique that has previously only been used by some spacecraft travelling to Earth's moon.
